title: Oil and gas markets’ perilous dilemma | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Wood Mackenzie's Alan Gelder lays out a binary scenario tree for oil and gas markets amid renewed Gulf/Red Sea conflict: no US-Iran deal risks Brent retesting $120/bbl and tipping the world into recession, while a credible deal could send Brent well below $60/bbl by 2027 as UAE and Iranian supply return to a market heading toward glut.

insights.claim: Iran has widened the Gulf conflict by enlisting Houthi proxies in Yemen to disrupt roughly 4 million b/d of Saudi Arabian crude exports transiting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, the alternative route used when the Strait of Hormuz is blocked.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Watch Red Sea shipping and tanker-insurance rates plus Saudi export volumes as a leading indicator of renewed supply stress beyond just the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.quote: enlisting its Houthi proxies in Yemen to disrupt around 4 million b/d of Saudi Arabia’s crude exports
insights.locator: The on-off-on conflict in the Gulf

insights.claim: The brief US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) allowed a few weeks of oil and LNG value-chain recovery and inventory rebuild, but its collapse has returned markets to the same perilous state that existed before the MoU was signed.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Diplomatic on/off cycles are now a primary near-term price driver; treat MoU status as a binary catalyst to track rather than assume a stable de-escalation.
insights.quote: oil and LNG markets are once again perilously placed, and the world is back to where it was before the MoU

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie frames the US-Iran standoff as a binary dilemma with huge global implications: either the conflict festers and produces dire economic consequences, or the two sides strike a sustainable deal that unlocks constrained oil and LNG supply.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Positioning should be scenario-based around this binary outcome rather than assuming gradual, linear de-escalation.
insights.quote: a binary outcome with huge implications for the world: allow the conflict to fester and face dire economic consequences or strike a sustainable deal to unlock constrained supply back into the market
insights.locator: The dilemma confronting the two sides

themes.theme: Bear Case: No Deal, Global Recession

insights.claim: In the no-deal scenario, up to 12 million b/d of liquids (12% of global production) and 86 Mt of LNG production (20% of global LNG) could be shut in, raising the risk of value-chain degradation including reservoir deterioration.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Extended shut-ins risk permanent reservoir damage, meaning some capacity may not return even after a deal is reached — a structural bullish tail risk to watch for.
insights.quote: Up to 12 million b/d of liquids (12% of the global production market) and 86 Mt of LNG production (20%) are shut in

insights.claim: Cushing crude inventories are already near operational minimums, so further inventory draws in a no-deal scenario would directly reduce the volume of US crude available to export markets.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: US export availability is itself a tightening constraint, not just a Gulf supply story — watch weekly Cushing stock data as a supplementary stress gauge.
insights.quote: Visible inventories at Cushing are already near operational minimums, reducing the volumes of US crude available to export markets.

insights.claim: Late-summer seasonality compounds the no-deal scenario because the northern hemisphere is at its peak of global oil demand, unlike the seasonal backdrop of earlier price spikes during this conflict.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Seasonal demand timing amplifies this disruption's price impact versus prior flare-ups, a reason this leg of the conflict could push prices higher than earlier ones.
insights.quote: Different seasonal factors are at play compared with earlier spikes, with late summer in the northern hemisphere traditionally the peak of global oil demand.
insights.locator: Upward pressure mounts on energy prices

insights.claim: China is responding to elevated import prices by drawing down its strategic oil reserves rather than paying up for crude imports, a move Wood Mackenzie says only delays rather than resolves the market reckoning.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: China's SPR drawdown is masking true import demand; a later reserve refill would add a fresh demand shock on top of the Gulf disruption.
insights.quote: China switching to tap its strategic oil reserves rather than pay up for crude imports at elevated prices only stalls the reckoning.
insights.locator: Upward pressure mounts on energy prices

insights.claim: In the no-deal case, Brent is forecast to return to the prior 2026 peaks of around $120/bbl (from March/April) and climb higher still, with demand destruction the only mechanism left to rebalance the market.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A $120+/bbl retest is the explicit bear-case price target to hedge against if Gulf talks collapse again.
insights.quote: Brent futures return to the previous US$120/bbl peaks of March and April before climbing higher still. Demand destruction is the only means to ultimately deliver market balance.
insights.locator: Brent futures return to the previous

insights.claim: Without Gulf LNG exports, European gas storage risks running dangerously low ahead of winter, and LNG prices could rise to demand-destroying levels that push Asian importers to switch to coal.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: European winter gas security and Asian fuel-switching to coal are both downstream risks of a prolonged Gulf conflict, relevant for gas and coal positioning.
insights.quote: Tight LNG supply, absent Gulf exports, threatens to leave European gas storage dangerously low ahead of winter.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's bear case sees high energy prices tipping the global economy into a shallow recession in H2 2026, deepening into a scarring recession into 2027 if the conflict persists.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: This is a macro recession call tied directly to Gulf conflict duration, a reason to hedge broad risk assets rather than only energy exposure.
insights.quote: high energy prices push the global economy into shallow recession in H2 2026. Prolonged high prices persisting towards the end of the year plunge the world into a deeper recession into 2027, scarring the global economy.

themes.theme: Bull Case: Deal Struck, Brent Slumps

insights.claim: If a credible deal is brokered, Wood Mackenzie expects a repeat of the June MoU market reaction: Brent falling off a cliff as investors unwind long positions built on bets for higher oil and refined product prices.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A credible-deal headline is a short-Brent/fade-the-spike catalyst, based on the precedent already observed once this cycle.
insights.quote: A market reaction similar to the June signing of the MoU. Reopening export routes leads to Brent immediately falling off a cliff, investors bailing from positions that bet on higher oil and refined product prices.

insights.claim: Even after a deal, a volatility window follows while the market judges the deal's durability, the risk of flare-ups, and the relative speed of oil supply versus demand recovery.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Do not expect an immediate clean re-rating post-deal; position for elevated realized volatility even in the bullish scenario.
insights.quote: A period of volatility ensues as the market assesses the sustainability of the deal, monitors the risk of flare ups and the likely variance between the speed of demand and supply recovery.

insights.claim: With the UAE now outside OPEC and free of production quotas, plus permanent removal of US sanctions opening a wider customer base for Iranian oil, the market could become awash with oil once a deal normalizes production and vessel flows.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Structural post-deal oversupply catalysts (UAE outside OPEC, unconstrained Iranian output) argue for fading any deal-driven price recovery beyond the initial drop.
insights.quote: With the UAE out of OPEC and freed from production constraints, and the permanent removal of US sanctions on Iran’s oil exports opening up a wider customer base to support Iranian production growth, the market could be awash with oil.

insights.claim: In the deal scenario, Wood Mackenzie projects Brent sinking well below $60/bbl into 2027, and says a diminished OPEC+ must act decisively or face certain further price declines if it instead competes for market share.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Sub-$60 Brent is the explicit bull-case (deal) price target; watch for coordinated OPEC+ supply cuts as the signal it is trying to defend that floor.
insights.quote: Brent sinks well below US$60/bbl into 2027. A diminished OPEC+ needs to act decisively to avoid much lower prices that are a certainty if the group elects to compete for market share.

themes.theme: Path to a Deal: Political Calculus

insights.claim: Despite mutual incentives to negotiate, a deal is far from assured: Iran's economic pressure is mounting now that MoU-era export revenues are gone, and Tehran wants a nuclear settlement close in substance to the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA).
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A durable deal likely requires nuclear-file concessions resembling the 2015 JCPOA, a much harder ask than a narrow export/sanctions swap, raising the bar for what counts as a 'credible deal.'
insights.quote: a nuclear solution close in substance to the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action it signed in 2015 is a big one

insights.claim: For the US, pressure to strike a deal is as much domestic as geopolitical: with midterm elections roughly 15 weeks away and gasoline near $4/gallon, the Republican party has a strong incentive to avoid contesting the vote with the conflict unresolved.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: The US midterm election timing (roughly mid-November 2026) is a concrete political deadline that could force Washington toward a deal; track it as a catalyst window.
insights.quote: It is difficult to believe that the Republican party would relish contesting the mid-term elections in just 15 weeks with the conflict unresolved and gasoline prices at US$4/gallon or more.
insights.locator: For the US, geopolitics is one thing
